title: Suboccipital Triangle, Curvatures and Spinal Puncture

steps.tx: Deep in the posterior neck beneath semispinalis capitis lies the muscular compartment designated the **suboccipital triangle**. Bounded by rectus capitis posterior major medially, obliquus capitis superior superolaterally, and obliquus capitis inferior inferolaterally, its floor is formed by the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and the posterior arch of the atlas.
steps.say: Deep in the upper neck beneath semispinalis capitis lies the suboccipital triangle. Bounded by rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior, and obliquus capitis inferior, its floor is formed by the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and the atlas arch.

vis.alt: Suboccipital region and atlanto-occipital membrane floor
vis.caption: Cervical spine relationships and suboccipital anatomy. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The contents of the suboccipital triangle comprise the horizontal third part of the vertebral artery and the **suboccipital nerve**, which represents the dorsal ramus of C1. The suboccipital nerve is purely motor, supplying all four suboccipital muscles. In contrast, the greater occipital nerve from the dorsal ramus of C2 emerges below obliquus capitis inferior.
steps.say: The suboccipital triangle contains the horizontal segment of the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve, the dorsal ramus of C1. This nerve provides purely motor supply to the suboccipital muscles, whereas the greater occipital nerve emerges below the inferior oblique.

steps.tx: The adult human vertebral column exhibits four sagittal curvatures that optimize balance and shock absorption. The primary thoracic and sacral curves show anterior concavity, or **kyphosis**, preserved from the original fetal C-shaped curvature. Primary kyphoses are determined by the wedge-like shape of the thoracic vertebral bodies.
steps.say: The adult spine exhibits four sagittal curves that optimize shock absorption. The thoracic and sacral curves maintain an anterior concavity, termed kyphosis, which is retained from the embryonic posture. These primary curves are shaped by wedged thoracic bodies.

steps.tx: Secondary curves display anterior convexity, designated **lordosis**, developing postnatally in response to gravity and motor milestones. Cervical lordosis appears at three to four months as the infant learns to hold the head upright. Lumbar lordosis develops around twelve to eighteen months when the toddler initiates standing and upright bipedal walking.
steps.say: Secondary curves exhibit an anterior convexity termed lordosis, developing after birth as motor milestones are reached. Cervical lordosis emerges when the infant learns to hold up the head, while lumbar lordosis develops as the toddler begins standing and walking.

steps.tx: To safely sample cerebrospinal fluid or deliver spinal anaesthesia, a clinician performs a **lumbar puncture** below the termination of the adult spinal cord. Because the spinal cord ends at the lower border of L1 in adults, a lumbar puncture needle is introduced at the L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace into the lumbar cistern.
steps.say: To obtain cerebrospinal fluid or administer spinal anaesthesia, a clinician performs a lumbar puncture below the spinal cord termination. Because the cord terminates at the lower border of L1 in adults, the needle safely enters at the L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace.

vis.alt: Lumbar puncture positioning, landmarks, and needle trajectory
vis.caption: Lumbar puncture procedure showing interspinous landmarking. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Landmarking the L3-L4 intervertebral space relies upon the **Tuffier line**, an imaginary transverse plane connecting the highest points of both iliac crests. This line reliably crosses the spine at the L4 spinous process or the L4-L5 interspinous space. In infants, the spinal cord terminates lower at L3, demanding special caution during spinal tap.
steps.say: Identifying the safe interspace relies on the Tuffier line, drawn horizontally across the highest summits of the iliac crests. This line crosses at the L4 spinous process or L4-L5 interspace. In infants, the cord extends down to L3, requiring a lower approach.

vis.alt: Spinal cord termination and lumbar cistern anatomy
vis.caption: Spinal cord termination, lumbar cistern, and CSF sampling. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: During a lumbar puncture, the spinal needle traverses distinct tissue layers in strict anatomical sequence: skin, subcutaneous fat, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, and the **ligamentum flavum**. Penetrating the elastic ligamentum flavum produces a characteristic tactile giving way, followed immediately by puncture of the dural-arachnoid membrane into the subarachnoid space.
steps.say: Advancing a lumbar puncture needle traverses specific layers in order: skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, and the ligamentum flavum. Piercing the resilient ligamentum flavum yields a distinct pop, after which the dura is entered.

steps.tx: Excessive or pathological spinal curvature impairs biomechanics: exaggerated thoracic kyphosis causes a hunchback posture, while exaggerated lumbar lordosis is common in late pregnancy and obesity. Lateral deviation of the vertebral column accompanied by vertebral rotation is classified as **scoliosis**, which distorts the thoracic rib cage and compromises respiratory mechanics.
steps.say: Excessive curvatures impair spinal mechanics: accentuated thoracic kyphosis produces a hunchback, while accentuated lumbar lordosis occurs in pregnancy and obesity. Lateral spinal curvature with vertebral rotation is scoliosis, which distorts the rib cage and restricts breathing.
